title: What is the difference between Short Polling (client keeps asking server every few seconds: simple but wasteful), Long Polling (client asks, server holds the connection until new data arrives: better but still HTTP overhead), SSE (Server-Sent Events: one-way server→client stream over HTTP), and WebSocket (full two-way communication over a single TCP connection)?
shortTitle: What is the difference between Short Polling, Long Polling, SSE, and WebSocket
keyPoints: Short polling asks the server on a fixed interval; simple but wasteful because most responses are empty.
Long polling holds the request open until data arrives or a timeout; reduces empty responses but still costs an HTTP cycle per update.
SSE is a one-way server-to-client stream over a single HTTP connection with automatic reconnection via EventSource.
WebSocket upgrades to a full-duplex channel on one TCP connection; both sides send freely, but infrastructure must be WebSocket-aware.
Use the least powerful technique that meets the need: SSE for server-push, WebSocket for two-way, polling as a fallback.
In banking, a stock ticker is SSE, a trading terminal is WebSocket, and a rarely changing status can use polling.

s1_definition.oneliner: Short polling asks repeatedly and wastes calls, long polling holds the request until data arrives, SSE is a one-way server-to-client stream, and WebSocket is a full two-way channel on one connection.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Short polling** – the client sends an HTTP request every few seconds; the server responds immediately, usually with nothing new; simple but wasteful at scale.
- **Long polling** – the client sends a request and the server holds it open until data is ready or a timeout; reduces empty responses but each update costs a full HTTP cycle.
- **SSE (Server-Sent Events)** – a one-way server-to-client stream over a single long-lived HTTP connection; the browser's `EventSource` API reconnects automatically.
- **WebSocket** – an HTTP upgrade to a full-duplex channel over one TCP connection; both sides send messages freely with minimal per-message overhead.
s1_definition.analogy: Rajesh is waiting for a transfer to clear at National Bank of India. Short polling is Rajesh phoning every ten seconds asking "is it done yet?" Long polling is Rajesh phoning and the clerk saying "stay on the line until it clears." SSE is the bank opening a one-way loudspeaker to Rajesh. WebSocket is a two-way open phone line where both Rajesh and the clerk speak whenever they like.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  Short Polling:     Client ──req──→ Server ──resp──→ (empty)
                     Client ──req──→ Server ──resp──→ (empty)
                     Client ──req──→ Server ──resp──→ (data!)

  Long Polling:      Client ──req──→ Server ......... (holds)
                                     Server ──resp──→ (data!)
                     Client ──req──→ (repeat)

  SSE:               Client ──connect──→ Server
                                  ←──event1──
                                  ←──event2──
                                  ←──event3──  (one-way stream)

  WebSocket:         Client ──upgrade──→ Server ──101──→
                     Client ←──msg──→ Server  (both ways, freely)
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
These are four techniques for delivering updates from server to client, on a spectrum from simplest to most capable. Short polling asks on a fixed interval and is trivial but wasteful. Long polling holds the request until data arrives, reducing empty responses but still costing an HTTP cycle per update. SSE is a true one-way push where the server streams events over one persistent HTTP connection with automatic reconnection built into the browser's EventSource API. WebSocket is a full-duplex channel where both sides send freely after an HTTP upgrade, ideal for interactive two-way traffic.

At National Bank of India, each feature uses the matching technique. An old dashboard short-polled transfer status and flooded the server, so it moved to long polling. The stock price ticker and payment notifications are one-way, so they stream with SSE. The live trading terminal needs two-way messaging at low latency, so it uses WebSocket.

The principle is to use the least powerful technique that meets the need. If the server only pushes to the client, SSE beats WebSocket for simplicity and free reconnection. If both sides must talk interactively, WebSocket is required. Polling is a fallback for simple cases. If a mostly-one-way feature needs an occasional client action, that action is a normal REST call alongside the SSE stream.

Remember one sentence: match the update technique to the direction of the data: polling for simple checks, SSE for server push, WebSocket for two-way, and always prefer the simplest one that works.
